newsitem.title: USA: Fargo Oscar wins bring smiles in namesake city.
newsitem.headline: Fargo Oscar wins bring smiles in namesake city.

text.p: News that its namesake movie had won two Oscars brought out a swell of civic pride in Fargo on Tuesday, nearly pushing the area's troubles with spring flooding off the front page of the local newspaper.

No matter that the movie largely takes place in Minnesota and is populated by people with Wisconsin accents or that some in the region had accused it of painting a simplistic picture of small town life. And forget that most of the Oscar night attention went to the epic "The English Patient."
Fargo was, as one T-shirt slogan said, "Winner for Best Town in a Title Role."

"It's wonderful," said Lola Holland, acting president of the Fargo Chamber of Commerce. "It has already been a boost for the community. Fargo is well known for many things, particularly the quality of life, but even at that we may be somewhat of a best-kept secret," she told Reuters.
As to those who thought the movie held the region up to a bad light, she said, "It's important that we all keep our sense of humour ... we do have a strong Scandinavian background here."

A sense of humour may have been particularly important hours before Monday's Academy Awards ceremonies when three more inches (7.6 cm) of snow fell on Fargo, bringing to 109.6 inches (278.4 cm) the season's total. Great, melting, brown mounds of snow line the streets and a season of passing ploughs has stacked some of it nearly to the eaves of buildings close by roads.

Townspeople celebrated the selection of Frances McDormand as best actress for her role in "Fargo" and Ethan and Joel Coen for best original screenplay. Gathering at the old Fargo movie theatre, guests wore big fur hats with ear flaps and other winter gear featured in the movie.

"It was a night to be proud of Scandinavian accents, drag out the duck boots and eat lefse (a thin potato bread) as movie fans gathered in the historic theatre," the Fargo Forum told its readers on Tuesday.
"I hope they do a sequel," Holland said. "Maybe they should call it West Fargo (the town which abuts Fargo)."
A radio talk show host, however, told his listeners on Tuesday he had heard the sequel had already been named. "It's called 'The Norwegian-American Patient,'" he said.
